# Math/Stats Application Workshop: R

Sections:

1. Data Import
2. Data checks and cleaning
3. 1-Tail Hypothesis Test: Is everyone signing onto all 3 agreements?
4. 2-Tail Hypothesis Test: Are Canada's emissions average?
5. Proportion Comparison Test: Are high-income countries more likely to make emission reduction pledges?
6. 2-Tail Means Comparison: Do high-income countries make higher or lower absolute emission reductions?
7. Group Comparisons: Are average emission levels different by continent?
8. Regression: Is there evidence of an Environmental Kuznets Curve?

Resources:

- [Hypothesis Testing in R](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2022/12/hypothesis-testing-in-r/#:~:text=Hypothesis%20Testing%20in%20R%2C%20A,are%20demonstrated%20in%20this%20course.&text=Each%20type%20of%20test%20can,test().)
- [Introduction to Econometrics With R](https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/)
- run `?fn` for R functions, and get their documentation in the bottom-right frame.
- search for a function's documentation on https://www.rdocumentation.org/


## How to read this document

Everything you did yesterday in Python has a direct R translation. The statistics
do not change. Only the syntax does. Four pieces of R vocabulary carry most of
the load, so learn them now.

**Function.** A named piece of code you call with round brackets: `mean(x)`
calls the function `mean` on the input `x`. The things you put inside the
brackets are its **arguments**. Arguments can be given by position
(`t.test(pledges, 3)`) or by name (`t.test(x = pledges, mu = 3)`). Name them.
Named arguments do not depend on order, and six months from now you will still
be able to read the line.

**Assignment.** `<-` stores a result under a name. `policy_df <- read_csv(...)`
runs `read_csv` and parks the answer in `policy_df`. R also accepts `=` for
this, but `<-` is the convention and it never gets confused with a named
argument. Nothing is printed when you assign; type the name on its own line to
see the object.

**Vector.** The basic R container: an ordered run of values that are all the
same type. `c(1, 4, 9)` builds a numeric vector of length 3, `c("a", "b")` a
character vector of length 2. Almost every R function is written to take a whole
vector at once, so `sqrt(c(1, 4, 9))` returns `1 2 3` with no loop. Python's
closest analogue is a NumPy array, not a list.

**Data frame.** A rectangle of data: a named collection of equal-length vectors
stacked side by side as columns. One column is one variable, one row is one
observation. This is R's version of a pandas DataFrame. The `tidyverse` uses a
slightly polished data frame called a **tibble**, which prints only the first 10
rows and tells you each column's type. Pull a single column out as a vector with
the dollar sign: `policy_df$year`.

Two more you will meet in a moment: the **pipe** `%>%`, which chains steps
together, and **NA**, R's marker for a missing value.


```{r}
# package import
# load tidyverse library and here packages
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, here, lmtest, sandwich)
```

A **package** is a bundle of extra functions somebody else wrote. R ships with a
core set (base R), and everything else you install once and then load in each
session. `pacman::p_load()` does install-if-missing and load in one step, so
this notebook runs on a fresh machine.

The `::` in `pacman::p_load` means "the `p_load` function from the `pacman`
package". You can always qualify a function this way, which is useful when two
packages define the same name.

What the four packages give us:

- **tidyverse**: not one package but a set that loads together. `readr` for
  reading files, `dplyr` for manipulating data frames, `ggplot2` for graphics,
  `tidyr` for reshaping, `tibble`, `stringr`, `forcats`, `purrr`.
- **here**: builds file paths starting from the project root, so a path that
  works on your laptop also works on mine.
- **lmtest**: `coeftest()`, for re-testing regression coefficients with a
  different variance estimate.
- **sandwich**: `vcovHC()`, the heteroskedasticity-robust variance estimator we
  feed into `coeftest()`.




# 1. Data Import

```{r}
# import data

# here() builds an absolute path from the project root. It finds that root by
# looking for a marker file: the r_applications.Rproj sitting next to this .Rmd
# is one such marker. That works when this folder is the open project.
#
# If R was started somewhere else (say the top of the Git repository), here()
# locks onto that other root and the CSV will not be there. The second line is
# the fallback: when knitting, knitr sets the working directory to the folder
# holding this .Rmd, so the bare filename always resolves.
csv_path <- here("policy_analysis.csv")
if (!file.exists(csv_path)) csv_path <- "policy_analysis.csv"

# show_col_types = FALSE suppresses the block of text readr otherwise prints
# describing how it guessed each column's type. We check the types ourselves in
# the next section.
policy_df <- read_csv(csv_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# print data head
head(policy_df)
```

`read_csv()` is `readr`'s CSV reader. It differs from base R's `read.csv()` in
three ways that matter: it is much faster on large files, it returns a tibble,
and it never silently converts text columns into factors.

`head()` shows the first 6 rows. Because the object is a tibble, the printout
also carries the dimensions and a type abbreviation under every column name:
`<chr>` for character (text), `<dbl>` for double (a number with decimals).

Two things to notice in that printout. The tibble is 10388 rows by 47 columns,
so this is country-year panel data: one row per country per year, 212 countries
from 1970 to 2018. And several columns already show `NA`, R's marker for a
missing value. `NA` is not zero and not an empty string. It is "we do not know",
and it propagates: `1 + NA` is `NA`, and `mean(c(1, 2, NA))` is `NA`. That
propagation is a feature, not a nuisance. It stops a missing value from quietly
turning into a wrong number.





# 2. Data Checks and Cleaning Approach

We want to check through our dataset before we start analyzing it, or else we're going to waste a lot of time later diverting back and fixing it.

What do we need to look at?

1. Checking column data types. Are numerics in float/int format?
2. Checking for missing values. Which columns and rows have them? How do we handle this?

### Column data types

Before that chunk runs, three pieces of syntax.

The **pipe**, `%>%`, takes whatever is on its left and passes it as the first
argument of the function on its right. `policy_df %>% summarise(...)` is exactly
`summarise(policy_df, ...)`. It exists so that a five-step transformation reads
top to bottom in the order it happens, instead of inside out. R 4.1 and later
also has a built-in pipe written `|>`; the two behave the same for our purposes.

`summarise()` collapses a data frame down to a single row of computed values.

`across()` applies the same function to many columns at once. `everything()` is
a selection helper meaning "all columns", so `across(everything(), typeof)`
means "run `typeof` on every column".

```{r}
# check types

policy_df %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), typeof))
```

These are mostly `doubles`, which are the correct numeric data types. The others are `character`, equivalent to Python's string data type.

Read the result as a one-row table whose entries are type names rather than
data. `double` is R's ordinary numeric type, a 64-bit floating point number.
`character` is text. R also has `integer` (whole numbers only) and `logical`
(`TRUE`/`FALSE`), neither of which appears here: `read_csv` stores whole numbers
such as `year` and `partytopledge1` as doubles, which is fine for arithmetic.

Only `cntry`, `country`, `CountryCode`, `wbregion` and `Incomegroup` are
character. Every other column is numeric and ready for arithmetic, so nothing
needs converting.

There is a fifth type worth naming now because it appears later: a **factor**.
A factor is a character column that R treats as a fixed set of categories, with
the distinct values stored as **levels**. Statistical functions need this
distinction. When we run the ANOVA in section 7, R has to know that `wbregion`
is seven groups and not seven pieces of text, and `aov()` converts the character
column to a factor for us.

```{r}
# getting column names

colnames(policy_df)
```
These are the same as in Python!

`colnames()` returns a character vector of the 47 column names. The numbers in
square brackets on the left of the printout are position indices, telling you
that the item after `[13]` is the thirteenth name. R indexes from 1, not from 0.

The names worth memorizing for today:

- `country`, `year`, `wbregion`, `Incomegroup`: identifiers and grouping
  variables.
- `partytopledge1`, `partytopledge2`, `partytopledge3`: 1 if the country is a
  party to the Kyoto, Copenhagen and Paris agreements respectively, 0 if not.
- `rel_reduction_low3`, `rel_reduction_high3`: the low and high emission
  reduction pledged under the third agreement (Paris), in percent.
- `GHG_percapita`: greenhouse gas emissions per person.
- `GDP_percapita`: GDP per person.

### Missing values

Regarding missing data, we know from our Python work that there's plenty of it. Again, we'll just be removing `NAN` data en masse.

`is.na(x)` returns a logical vector the same length as `x`, with `TRUE` wherever
the value is missing. `sum()` on a logical vector counts the `TRUE`s, because R
treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0. So `sum(is.na(.x))` is the number of
missing values in a column.

The `~ sum(is.na(.x))` part is a **lambda**, an unnamed function written inline.
The tilde starts it, and `.x` stands for whichever column `across()` is
currently handing over. You need it here because we are not just naming an
existing function, we are building a small one on the spot.

```{r}
# missingness check

policy_df %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

# lots!
```
Our takeaway is that we've got plenty of missing values, in plenty of columns!

A 47-column-wide row of numbers is hard to scan. The same information as a
picture is easier. To draw it, we first have to turn that wide one-row result
into a long two-column one, because `ggplot2` wants one row per thing you intend
to draw.

That reshaping is what **tidy data** means. A dataset is tidy when each variable
is a column and each observation is a row. Here the observation is "a column of
`policy_df`" and the variables are its name and its missing count, so tidy form
is 47 rows of two columns. `pivot_longer()` does the conversion: it takes the
column names into one new column (`names_to`) and the values into another
(`values_to`).

```{r missing-plot}
# Reshape the one-row summary into one row per column of policy_df.
missing_counts <- policy_df %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to  = "column",     # new column holding the old column names
    values_to = "n_missing"   # new column holding the counts
  ) %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0)       # keep only columns that actually have gaps

# A ggplot is built by adding layers with `+`:
#   ggplot(data, aes(...)) sets the data and maps columns to visual positions
#   geom_col()             draws one bar per row, with height taken from y
#   coord_flip()           swaps the axes so the long names stay readable
#   labs()                 sets the title and the axis labels
# reorder(column, n_missing) sorts the bars by height instead of alphabetically.
ggplot(missing_counts, aes(x = reorder(column, n_missing), y = n_missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Missing values are concentrated in a few columns",
    subtitle = "28 of the 47 columns contain at least one NA; 10388 rows in total",
    x = "Column",
    y = "Number of rows with NA"
  )
```

Read the bar chart as a triage list. 28 of the 47 columns have gaps, and the
damage is very uneven. `upperbound2` is missing in 8624 of 10388 rows, so it is
effectively unusable. `upperbound1` (7595) is next, then `cpi_inflation` (3610), `upperbound3`
(3479) and `oil_rents` (2950). The variables we actually need are in better shape: `GHG_percapita` is
missing 728 times, `GDP_percapita` 2397, `partytopledge3` 1372, `wbregion` 196.
This is why the cleaning plan below is per-question rather than global. Dropping
every row with any `NA` anywhere would throw away most of the panel to protect
columns we never touch.

### Data Cleaning Plan

We could come up with a general criteria for which rows stay and which we get rid of, to keep a common and standard dataframe. This may involve removing all countries with missing data (a strict approach), or just removing years with missing data, or a combined approach.

However, our focus today is on Hypothesis Testing, with a side of Data Cleaning. So, our process will be to keep all data in the base `policy_df` DataFrame. When we're working on each specific exercise, we'll limit it just to the columns we need to use, and then remove all rows with missing data. This lets us test Hypotheses with the maximum range of available data, and try out data cleaning along the way.

Two functions do the row dropping, and they are near-synonyms here:

- `na.omit()` is base R. It drops every row containing an `NA` in any column.
- `drop_na()` is from `tidyr`. With no arguments it behaves like `na.omit()`.
  Given column names, as in `drop_na(GHG_percapita)`, it drops rows missing only
  in those columns and leaves the rest alone.

Both appear below, because the author used whichever was to hand. Prefer
`drop_na()` with explicit column names in your own work: it states which
variables the analysis depends on, so the row count cannot silently change when
an unrelated column gains a gap.

One consequence to keep in front of you all day. Because each section drops rows
on its own terms, each section works with a different set of countries. Section
3 gets 184, section 4 gets 209 plus Canada, section 6 gets 150. The samples are
not interchangeable and the results are not directly comparable across sections.



# 3. 1-Tail Hypothesis Test: Are all countries signing onto all 3 agreements?

We'll use this question to see whether there is a high degree of consensus among the agreements being desirable. With a one-sided test, we'll see if most countries sign up onto all 3, or if there is significant non-acceptance.

### What a hypothesis test actually does

This is the part of the workshop people find hardest, so read this before the
code rather than after it.

We have 184 countries. We can compute their average number of signed agreements
exactly, and it is 1.663. There is no uncertainty about that number: it is
arithmetic on the data in front of us. So what is left to test?

The answer is that we are not really interested in these 184 countries as such.
We treat them as one draw from a wider process that could have come out
differently, and we want a claim about that process. A different draw would give
a slightly different average. The question is whether the gap between what we
observed and what some benchmark claims is bigger than the wobble we would
expect from the draw alone.

**The null hypothesis, H0**, is the boring benchmark, stated as a specific
number so that we can compute with it. Here: the true mean number of signed
agreements is 3. The null is what we assume while doing the arithmetic. We never
prove it.

**The alternative, H1**, is what we would conclude instead if the data are hard
to square with H0. Here: the true mean is below 3.

**The test statistic** measures the distance from the data to the null, in units
of the data's own noise. For a mean, that is the t-statistic:

```
t = (sample mean - null value) / (sample standard deviation / sqrt(n))
```

The denominator is the **standard error**, the typical amount the sample mean
would bounce around from one draw to the next. Dividing by it makes the number
comparable across problems. A t of -2 means "two standard errors below the
null", whether we are measuring emissions or exam scores.

**The p-value** is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as
extreme as the one we got, *if H0 were true*. Small p means the data would be
surprising under H0.

Now the sentence that matters most, because it is the one people get wrong. The
p-value is **not** the probability that H0 is true. It is not the probability
you are wrong. It is a statement about the data given the hypothesis, not about
the hypothesis given the data. Two consequences follow:

- A large p-value is not evidence that H0 is true. It means the data did not
  contradict it. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and with a
  small sample almost nothing contradicts anything.
- A small p-value says the data are unlikely under H0. It says nothing about
  whether the difference is large enough to matter. With 7000 observations, a
  difference too small to care about will still be "significant".

Always report the estimate and the confidence interval alongside the p-value.
The p-value answers "could this be noise?". The interval answers "how big is
it?", which is usually the question you actually had.

**One-tailed versus two-tailed.** This is a choice about where you are willing
to look for a departure from H0, and it must be made before you see the result.

- Two-tailed (`alternative = "two.sided"`) asks: is the true mean different from
  the null value, in either direction? The 5% is split into 2.5% in each tail.
- One-tailed (`alternative = "less"` or `"greater"`) asks about one direction
  only, and puts the whole 5% in that tail. It has more power to detect a
  departure in the direction you named, at the price of having none at all in
  the other direction.

Here `"less"` is defensible because 3 is the ceiling. There are exactly three
agreements, so a country cannot sign more than three and the true mean cannot
exceed 3. There is no upper tail to test. Note the trap: picking the tail after
seeing which way the data leaned roughly doubles your false-positive rate. That
is one of the researcher degrees of freedom problems discussed in section 6.

### Our Hypotheses

- H0: Effectively all countries sign up to all 3 agreements (Kyoto, Copenhagen, Paris)
- H1: Not all countries sign up to all 3 agreements

### Steps

We'll take one value from each country (all of their pledge agreements variables are the same across years), then sum the pledges they've made and compare with 3. In this case, a one-sided hypothesis test makes sense, as there are only these three agreements!



```{r}
# dataframe creation


# Select specific columns
hypothesis_1_df <- policy_df %>%
  select(country, year, partytopledge1, partytopledge2, partytopledge3)

# Display the first few rows
head(hypothesis_1_df)
```

`select()` keeps the named columns and drops the rest, in the order you list
them. It is `dplyr`'s column chooser, the counterpart to `filter()`, which
chooses rows. Note that it does not modify `policy_df`: it returns a new tibble,
which we assign to `hypothesis_1_df`. R functions almost never change their
inputs in place, so the original stays intact for the next section.

The three `partytopledge` columns are 0/1 indicators stored as doubles. Because
they are 0 and 1, adding them gives a count, and averaging them gives a
proportion. That is the trick we use in this section and again in section 5.

```{r}
# NaN check
missing_values <- hypothesis_1_df %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

print(missing_values)

# NaN removal
hypothesis_1_df <- hypothesis_1_df %>%
  na.omit()

hypothesis_1_df
```

The check shows 1372 missing values in each of the three pledge columns and none
in `country` or `year`. All three go missing together, which makes sense: the
gaps are whole countries that are not covered by the pledge data at all, not
scattered individual years.

`na.omit()` then drops those rows, taking the tibble from 10388 rows to 9016.
The line after it is just the object's name, which prints it. In an R Markdown
chunk, a bare expression on its own line is displayed; that is why some chunks
here use `print()` and some do not. They do the same thing.

Note that this reassigns `hypothesis_1_df` to itself. That is normal in a
pipeline, but it means re-running the chunk out of order operates on already
cleaned data. If a count ever looks wrong, restart R and run from the top.


There were three different rounds of environmental pledges involved in this dataset:

1. The Kyoto Protocol (signed 1997)
2. The Copenhagen Accord (signed 2009)
3. The Paris Agreement (signed 2016)

We'll combine all three variables in `total_pledges`, equal to the number of active agreements the country has signed onto.

```{r}
# Add a new column "total_pledges" as the sum of other columns
hypothesis_1_df <- hypothesis_1_df %>%
  mutate(total_pledges = partytopledge1 + partytopledge2 + partytopledge3)

hypothesis_1_df
```

`mutate()` adds a column (or overwrites one, if the name already exists) and
returns the whole data frame. The name on the left of `=` is the new column; the
expression on the right is evaluated row by row, using the other columns by bare
name with no quotes and no `policy_df$` prefix. That bare-name convention is
what makes `dplyr` compact, and it is the main way `dplyr` code differs in feel
from base R.

The arithmetic is **vectorized**: `partytopledge1 + partytopledge2` adds the two
columns element by element down all 9016 rows at once. There is no loop, and you
should not write one.

`total_pledges` now runs from 0 to 3.

```{r}
# Group by Country and take the first value of total_pledges for each country

hypothesis_1_sample_df <- hypothesis_1_df %>%
  select(country, total_pledges) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarize(total_pledges = first(total_pledges))

head(hypothesis_1_sample_df$total_pledges)

tail(hypothesis_1_sample_df$total_pledges)
```

This is the step that turns 9016 country-year rows into 184 country rows, and it
is the one to understand properly.

`group_by()` does not change the data. It attaches a label saying "from now on,
treat rows sharing a `country` value as one unit". `summarize()` then collapses
each of those units to a single row. So the pipeline says: split by country,
take one number per country, stack the results.

`first()` takes the first value in each group. That is legitimate *only* because
the pledge variables are constant within a country: signing the Paris Agreement
is a country-level fact recorded identically in every year's row. Verified: no
country has more than one distinct `total_pledges` value. If the variable did
move over time, `first()` would silently pick whichever year happened to sort
first, which is exactly the kind of bug that never announces itself.

Why collapse at all? Because the t-test assumes independent observations. Using
all 9016 rows would count Canada 49 times, once per year, and those 49 rows
carry no more information than 1. The sample size would be inflated by a factor
of roughly 49, the standard error would shrink by a factor of 7, and the
p-value would be meaninglessly small.

`head()` and `tail()` show the first and last 6 values: `2 1 2 1 2 2` and
`1 1 0 1 1 1`. The `$` extracts `total_pledges` as a plain numeric vector, which
is what `t.test()` wants.

The number counts, before we test anything:

```{r pledge-distribution}
# table() cross-tabulates: it counts how many times each distinct value occurs.
table(hypothesis_1_sample_df$total_pledges)

# Mean and standard deviation of the 184 country values.
mean(hypothesis_1_sample_df$total_pledges)
sd(hypothesis_1_sample_df$total_pledges)
```

```{r pledge-plot}
# factor() converts the 0/1/2/3 counts into categories, so ggplot draws four
# discrete bars instead of a continuous numeric axis.
#
# geom_bar() counts the rows itself, unlike geom_col() above which was handed
# heights directly. after_stat(count) reaches into those computed counts so we
# can print them on top of the bars.
ggplot(hypothesis_1_sample_df, aes(x = factor(total_pledges))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Most countries joined one or two of the three agreements",
    subtitle = "184 countries; sample mean 1.66, null hypothesis value 3",
    x = "Number of agreements signed (total_pledges)",
    y = "Number of countries"
  )
```

The bar chart is the whole result before any test is run. If the null were even
roughly right, nearly all 184 bars would sit over 3. Instead the mode is 1 (82
countries), 58 signed two, only 36 signed all three, and 8 signed none. The
sample mean of 1.66 is barely more than half the null value of 3, and the
spread (sd 0.84) is small relative to that gap. A test on this picture is a
formality, and the size of the t-statistic below reflects that.

### Q1 Hypothesis Testing


We will use the base R function, `t.test()`

It outputs a test statistic (i.e. t-value here) and an associated p-value.

Run the following line in the console to open the help page in the bottom-right frame. It is not evaluated when the document is knitted.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?t.test
```

The relevant arguments are:

- `x`: a numeric vector of data
- `mu`: the null hypothesis population average to compare to
- `alternative`: one of {"two.sided", "less", "greater"} for style of t-test

We can assign it to a variable called `test_result`, and then extract the t-stat and p-values with `$statistic` and `$p.value`

The chunk above is marked `eval=FALSE` in its header, which tells knitr to
display the code but not run it. `?t.test` opens a help viewer, which makes no
sense during a knit.

On the argument `alternative`, note that it describes H1, not H0. `"less"` means
"the alternative is that the true mean is less than `mu`", so the p-value is
computed from the left tail only. Getting this backwards is a common error and R
will not warn you.

One more thing about `test_result`. It is a **list**: a container that, unlike a
vector, can hold pieces of different types and shapes under names. `t.test()`
returns the statistic, the p-value, the degrees of freedom, the confidence
interval and the estimate all in one object. `$` pulls out one named piece, the
same operator that pulls a column out of a data frame. Run `names(test_result)`
in the console to see everything available.

```{r}
# Conduct one-sample t-test
test_result <- t.test(hypothesis_1_sample_df$total_pledges, mu = 3, alternative = "less")

# Extract test statistic and p-value
test_statistic <- test_result$statistic
p_value <- test_result$p.value

# Print results
cat("Test Statistic: ", test_statistic, "\n")
cat("P-value: ", p_value, "\n")
```

`cat()` prints its arguments joined together with no quotes and no `[1]` index
marker, which is why it is used instead of `print()` for these one-line reports.
`"\n"` is a newline; without it the next `cat()` would continue on the same
line.

### Q1: how to read this output

t = -21.591 and p = 1.67e-52. Take them one at a time.

The t-statistic is arithmetic you can check by hand:

```
standard error = 0.8399 / sqrt(184)      = 0.0619
t              = (1.6630 - 3) / 0.0619   = -21.59
```

So the sample mean sits about 21.6 standard errors below 3. For reference, the
5% one-tailed critical value at 183 degrees of freedom is about -1.65. We are
past it by an order of magnitude.

**Degrees of freedom** is 183, which is n - 1. One degree of freedom is spent
estimating the mean, so 183 independent pieces of information remain for
estimating the spread. The t distribution is wider than the normal at small df
to account for that extra uncertainty, and converges to the normal as df grows.

p = 1.67e-52 is scientific notation for 0.00000...167 with 51 zeros after the
decimal point. Read it as "essentially zero". Under H0, a sample this far below
3 would essentially never happen. We reject H0 at any conventional significance
level.

Do not over-read the tiny p-value. It does not mean the result is 52 times more
important than a p of 0.001. Below roughly 1e-10 the number is an artifact of
the assumed t distribution in a region no dataset can actually inform. All it
tells you is "not noise". The size of the effect is in the means: 1.66 against
3, a shortfall of 1.34 agreements per country.

The substantive conclusion: there is no near-universal consensus. Signing all
three is the exception, not the rule.

A caution about the model, since this is the first test. A t-test assumes the
sample mean is approximately normally distributed. Here the underlying variable
takes only the values 0, 1, 2 and 3, so it is nowhere near normal. That is
usually fine, because the Central Limit Theorem applies to the *mean*, not to
the raw data, and n = 184 is ample. It also barely matters here: no reasonable
adjustment moves a t of -21.6 anywhere near the boundary.


# 4. 2-Tail Hypothesis Test: Are Canada's emissions average?


Now we'll be doing a two-sided hypothesis test, where we compare a series of data points to a given value and test if the sample has a statistically significant difference. This time, it can be greater or less than the given value.

### Our Hypotheses

- H0: Most countries' average per-capita carbon emissions are equal to Canadian values
- H1: Most countries' average per-capita carbon emissions are not equal to Canadian values

### Steps

We are going to take Canada's average per capita carbon emissions and compare them to all other countries. Are other countries significantly greater or lower than us?

The structure differs from section 3 in exactly one respect: `alternative` is
left at its default of `"two.sided"`. We have no reason in advance to expect the
rest of the world to be above rather than below Canada, so we test for a
difference in either direction and split the 5% into 2.5% per tail.

Note what the test does and does not treat as uncertain. Canada's average is
plugged in as `mu`, a fixed known constant. The test therefore asks whether the
*other countries'* mean differs from that number. It does not put a standard
error on Canada's own average, so it is not a comparison of two samples. If you
wanted that, you would need a two-sample test on the underlying country-year
observations, which is a different question with a different answer.



```{r}

# Create hypothesis_2_df with selected columns
hypothesis_2_df <- policy_df %>%
  select(country, GHG_percapita)

# Group by country to get average emissions
hypothesis_2_df <- hypothesis_2_df %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(avg_emissions = mean(GHG_percapita))

# Split into Canada and non-Canada versions
hypothesis_2_canada <- hypothesis_2_df %>%
  filter(country == "Canada")

hypothesis_2_df <- hypothesis_2_df %>%
  filter(country != "Canada")

```

Four things happen in that chunk.

`drop_na()` removes the 728 rows where `GHG_percapita` is missing. Because we
selected only two columns first, no other column can trigger a drop.

`summarise(avg_emissions = mean(GHG_percapita))` collapses each country to one
row again, but this time with a genuine average over its years rather than
`first()`. `GHG_percapita` moves over time, so taking the first value would be a
choice about which year, and averaging is the honest summary. The result has a
new name, `avg_emissions`, which is worth noticing: from here on the column is
called `avg_emissions`, not `GHG_percapita`.

`filter()` keeps rows where a condition is `TRUE`. `==` tests equality and `!=`
tests inequality. Two equals signs, not one: a single `=` is assignment or a
named argument, and using it here is an error. `filter()` also drops `NA` rows
automatically, since `NA == "Canada"` is `NA`, not `TRUE`.

The two filters partition the 210 countries into Canada (1) and everyone else
(209). Reassigning `hypothesis_2_df` in the last step is the usual overwrite:
after this chunk the name refers to the 209, not the 210.

```{r}
head(hypothesis_2_df$avg_emissions)

tail(hypothesis_2_df$avg_emissions)
```

```{r}
hypothesis_2_canada
```

Canada's country-average per-capita emissions are 22.92. Compare that with the
first six non-Canada values printed above, which run from about 1.0 to 6.8.
Canada is not close to those. Whether that is a general pattern or six unlucky
draws is what the test settles.

Look at the distribution before testing it:

```{r emissions-distribution}
# Summary statistics for the 209 non-Canada countries.
summary(hypothesis_2_df$avg_emissions)

# How many countries emit more per person than Canada?
sum(hypothesis_2_df$avg_emissions > hypothesis_2_canada$avg_emissions)
```

```{r emissions-plot}
# geom_histogram bins a continuous variable and counts rows per bin.
# binwidth = 5 sets bins 5 tonnes wide; color = "white" outlines the bars.
# geom_vline draws a vertical reference line at a fixed x position.
ggplot(hypothesis_2_df, aes(x = avg_emissions)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(hypothesis_2_df$avg_emissions),
    color = "black", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = hypothesis_2_canada$avg_emissions,
    color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = 60, label = "Canada = 22.9",
           color = "red", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = 52, label = "World mean = 9.3", hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Canada sits in the right tail of the world emissions distribution",
    subtitle = "Country averages of GHG per capita, 209 countries excluding Canada",
    x = "Average GHG per capita (country mean over all available years)",
    y = "Number of countries"
  )
```

The histogram explains the test result before the test runs. The distribution is
severely right-skewed: 117 of the 209 countries fall below 5 and 143 fall below
7.5, the median is 3.99, and a thin tail stretches out past 180. The solid black line marks the
mean of 9.30, already pulled well above the median by that tail. The dashed red
line at Canada's 22.92 sits far to the right of the bulk. Only 14 of 209
countries emit more per person than Canada.

The skew matters for two reasons. First, "average" is ambiguous: Canada is 2.5
times the mean but 5.7 times the median. Second, the t-test relies on the
sampling distribution of the mean being roughly normal. With n = 209 that is a
reasonable bet even for skewed data, but with a much smaller sample it would
not be.


### Q2 Hypothesis Testing

This also uses the base R `t.test()` function.

```{r}
# Extract the GHG_percapita values for hypothesis_2_df and hypothesis_2_canada
hypothesis_2_df_values <- hypothesis_2_df$avg_emissions
hypothesis_2_canada_values <- hypothesis_2_canada$avg_emissions

# Conduct one-sample t-test
test_result <- t.test(hypothesis_2_df_values, mu = mean(hypothesis_2_canada_values))

# Extract test statistic and p-value
test_statistic <- test_result$statistic
p_value <- test_result$p.value

# Print results
cat("Test Statistic: ", test_statistic, "\n")
cat("P-value: ", p_value, "\n")
```

Two notes on the code. `hypothesis_2_canada_values` is a vector of length 1, so
`mean()` of it is just that one number; the call is harmless but the `mean()` is
doing nothing. And `alternative` is absent, so it defaults to `"two.sided"`,
which is what section 4 wants.

Also notice that `test_result` is being reused. The same name held the section 3
result. R overwrites it without complaint. That is fine as long as the document
is run top to bottom, and a trap if it is not.

### Q2 Interpretation?

t = -10.054, p = 1.24e-19, on 208 degrees of freedom. Reject H0.

The arithmetic again:

```
standard error = 19.584 / sqrt(209)       = 1.355
t              = (9.298 - 22.917) / 1.355 = -10.05
```

The negative sign says the rest of the world is *below* Canada. Because the test
is two-tailed, the p-value counts both tails: it is the probability of a t below
-10.05 plus the probability of a t above +10.05. That doubling is why a
two-tailed p-value is twice the corresponding one-tailed p-value for the same
data. Here doubling a number that small changes nothing.

Print the full object rather than just two extracted numbers, and you get the
piece that actually answers the economics:

```{r q2-full-output}
test_result
```

The 95 percent confidence interval is [6.63, 11.97]. Read it as the range of
null values that this sample would *not* reject. Canada's 22.92 is nowhere near
it. The interval is the useful output here, more so than the p-value: it says
the typical country emits somewhere between about 6.6 and 12.0 tonnes per
person, against Canada's 22.9. Canada is roughly twice the top of that range.

To make the two-tailed logic visible:

```{r t-distribution-plot}
# Build the t density curve for 208 degrees of freedom.
t_grid <- tibble(t = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 600)) %>%
  mutate(density = dt(t, df = 208))          # dt() = t probability density

# qt() is the inverse: the t value with 97.5% of the area to its left.
# For a two-tailed 5% test, reject outside plus or minus this value.
crit <- qt(0.975, df = 208)

ggplot(t_grid, aes(x = t, y = density)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(t_grid, t <= -crit), fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_area(data = filter(t_grid, t >=  crit), fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.1, y = 0.06, label = "reject H0\n2.5%",
           color = "firebrick", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.1, y = 0.06, label = "reject H0\n2.5%",
           color = "firebrick", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Two-tailed rejection regions, t distribution with 208 df",
    subtitle = paste0("Critical values at +/- ", round(crit, 3),
                      "; observed t = -10.05 is far off the left of this plot"),
    x = "t statistic",
    y = "Probability density"
  )
```

The curve is the distribution the t-statistic would follow if H0 were true. The
two shaded wedges hold 2.5% of the area each, and their inner edges are the
critical values at plus and minus 1.971. Any observed t landing in the red is
declared too unlikely under H0. Our observed t of -10.05 is not on this plot at
all: it is two and a half plot-widths further left. That distance is what
p = 1.24e-19 encodes.

Compare this picture with the one-tailed test in section 3, where the whole 5%
would sit in a single wedge on the left and the right tail would carry no
rejection region at all.



# 5. Proportion Comparison Test: Are high-income countries more likely to make emission reduction pledges?

The environmental Kuznets Curve suggests we might see an inverted-U relationship of carbon emissions with national wealth.

- at low wealth levels, countries don't produce enough to cause high carbon emissions

- at medium wealth levels, countries are focused on production over environmental concerns, leading to high per-capita emissions

- at high wealth levels, environmental concerns become emphasized and countries spend to reduce their emissions


We will investigate this effect by seeing whether High Income countries are more likely to sign onto the Paris Climate Agreement than poorer countries.

### Our Hypotheses

- H0: There is no difference in proportion signing the Agreement.
- H1: The proportion of High Income countries signing is different from non-High Income countries


### Steps:

1. Make dataframe of `country`, `Incomegroup`, `partytopledge3`
2. Subset out the High Income countries
3. Compute average for High Income, and not-High Income countries
4. Compare using statistical test

The outcome here is binary: a country either is or is not a party to the Paris
Agreement. `partytopledge3` codes that as 1 or 0, so the mean of the column *is*
the proportion of signatories. That is why the same `mean()` you have been using
for emissions now reads as a percentage.

`Incomegroup` is a World Bank classification with four values in this file:
"High income" (3381 rows), "Upper middle income" (2646), "Lower middle income"
(2205) and "Low income" (1470), plus 686 rows where it is missing. The code
below splits on "High income" versus everything else, which folds the three
lower categories into one comparison group.



```{r}
# Create hypothesis_3_df with selected columns
hypothesis_3_df <- policy_df %>%
  select(country, Incomegroup, partytopledge3)
```



```{r}
# creating High Income dataframe

# Create hypothesis_3_hi data frame by filtering Incomegroup
hypothesis_3_hi <- hypothesis_3_df %>%
  filter(Incomegroup == "High income")

# Remove rows with NA
hypothesis_3_hi <- hypothesis_3_hi %>%
  drop_na()

# Group by country and take the first value of pledge_proportion
hypothesis_3_hi_group <- hypothesis_3_hi %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(partytopledge3 = first(partytopledge3))



# creating not-High Income dataframe

# Create hypothesis_3_not_hi data frame by filtering Incomegroup
hypothesis_3_not_hi <- hypothesis_3_df %>%
  filter(Incomegroup != "High income")

# Remove rows with NA
hypothesis_3_not_hi <- hypothesis_3_not_hi %>%
  drop_na()

# Group by country and take the first value of pledge_proportion
hypothesis_3_not_hi_group <- hypothesis_3_not_hi %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(partytopledge3 = first(partytopledge3))

```

The two blocks are the same four steps run on complementary subsets: filter to
the income group, drop rows with missing values, then collapse to one row per
country by taking `first()`. As in section 3, `first()` is safe because
`partytopledge3` does not vary within a country.

Order matters in a way that is easy to miss. `filter()` runs before `drop_na()`,
so a country whose `Incomegroup` is missing is excluded from *both* groups: it
fails `== "High income"` and it fails `!= "High income"`, because a comparison
with `NA` returns `NA`, not `TRUE`. The two groups therefore do not have to add
up to the full country list, and they do not: 55 + 126 = 181, not 212.

The `summarise()` output keeps the name `partytopledge3` even though it now
holds one value per country rather than one per country-year. Reusing the name
is convenient and slightly misleading. `paris_member` would have been clearer.

```{r}
cat("Proportion of High Income countries signing Paris Climate Agreement: ", mean(hypothesis_3_hi_group$partytopledge3), "\n")
cat("Number of signatory high income countries: ", sum(hypothesis_3_hi_group$partytopledge3), "\n")
cat("Number of high income countries: ", length(hypothesis_3_hi_group$country), "\n")
```

```{r}
cat("Proportion of non-High Income countries signing Paris Climate Agreement: ", mean(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group$partytopledge3), "\n")
cat("Number of signatory non-high income countries: ", sum(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group$partytopledge3), "\n")
cat("Number of non-high income countries: ", length(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group$country), "\n")
```

Three functions on the same 0/1 column give three different readings of it.
`mean()` is the proportion, `sum()` is the count of 1s, and `length()` is the
number of countries. `length()` on the `country` column is a slightly indirect
way of asking for the row count; `nrow(hypothesis_3_hi_group)` says the same
thing more plainly.

The numbers: 53 of 55 high-income countries have joined (96.36%), and 121 of 126
others have (96.03%). The gap is 0.33 percentage points, which is two countries'
worth of rounding. There is nothing here for a test to find, and the point of
running one is to confirm that reading rather than to discover something.

```{r proportion-plot}
# Assemble a small tibble by hand with tibble(), one row per group. Building a
# two-row table like this is often the fastest way to get a summary into ggplot.
proportion_summary <- tibble(
  group  = c("High income", "Not high income"),
  signed = c(sum(hypothesis_3_hi_group$partytopledge3),
             sum(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group$partytopledge3)),
  total  = c(nrow(hypothesis_3_hi_group),
             nrow(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group))
) %>%
  mutate(proportion = signed / total)

pooled <- sum(proportion_summary$signed) / sum(proportion_summary$total)

ggplot(proportion_summary, aes(x = group, y = proportion, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pooled, linetype = "dashed") +
  # paste0() glues strings together with no separator; round() trims decimals.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(signed, " of ", total, " (",
                               round(100 * proportion, 1), "%)")),
            vjust = -0.5) +
  # Force the y axis onto the full 0-1 range so the bars are not misleading.
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(
    title = "Paris Agreement membership is near universal in both income groups",
    subtitle = paste0("Dashed line is the pooled proportion, ",
                      round(pooled, 4)),
    x = "Income group",
    y = "Proportion that joined the Paris Agreement"
  )
```

Both bars are essentially at the top of the chart and essentially at the same
height. That is the finding. The dashed pooled line at 0.9613 passes through
both bars. Drawing the y axis over its full 0 to 1 range is deliberate: had it
been auto-scaled to the range 0.960 to 0.964, the 0.33 percentage point gap
would have filled the plot and looked enormous. Truncated axes are the easiest
way to make a null result look like a discovery.

### Q3 Hypothesis Testing

This time, we're comparing two proportions with `prop.test()`

Proportions comparison tests in R are fairly similar to Python. We input two vectors, with total number (`n`) and number treated (`x`).

`n` holds the total numbers for each group

`x` is the number treated, or to which our condition of interest applies

So if we have 1000 electricians (250 of whom smoke), and 1000 doctors (190 of whom smoke), we would input their values as:

`x = c(250, 190), n = c(1000, 1000)`

We also use:

- `alternative`: just as in t-test, this is one of {"two.sided", "less", "greater"}

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?prop.test
```

Two more arguments matter here.

`correct` switches Yates' continuity correction on or off. The correction shrinks
the test statistic slightly to compensate for approximating a discrete count
distribution with a continuous curve. It is `TRUE` by default. Setting
`correct = FALSE` is what makes the R result match the uncorrected z-test that
`statsmodels.proportions_ztest()` computed in Python. Use `FALSE` when you want
that match; the default `TRUE` is the more conservative choice.

Note also that `c()` builds a vector, and the *order* of the two entries has to
be the same in `x` and in `n`. Here the first slot is high income and the second
is everyone else. Swapping one but not the other silently tests a different
hypothesis.

`prop.test()` reports a **chi-squared** statistic, not a z. For a two-group
comparison the two are related by `z = sqrt(chi-squared)`, which is why the
author takes a square root on the last line. The chi-squared version loses the
sign, so it cannot tell you which group was higher; read that off the two
proportions instead.

```{r}
# x: we have 53 signatory HI countries and 121 signatory non_HI countries
# n: we have 55 total HI countries and 126 total non-HI countries

z_test <- prop.test(x = c(53, 121), n = c(55, 126), alternative = "two.sided", correct = FALSE)

z_test

sqrt(z_test$statistic) # z-score


```

Those four counts are typed in by hand, copied from the two `cat()` blocks
above. That is fragile: change a filter upstream and the test keeps using the
old numbers without complaint. The same call driven off the data:

```{r prop-test-computed}
# Same test, with the counts read out of the data rather than typed in.
z_test_computed <- prop.test(
  x = c(sum(hypothesis_3_hi_group$partytopledge3),
        sum(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group$partytopledge3)),
  n = c(nrow(hypothesis_3_hi_group),
        nrow(hypothesis_3_not_hi_group)),
  alternative = "two.sided",
  correct = FALSE
)

cat("chi-squared:", z_test_computed$statistic, "\n")
cat("p-value:    ", z_test_computed$p.value, "\n")
# as.numeric() strips the "X-squared" name that R carries along, which would
# otherwise mislabel the z-score in the printout.
cat("z-score:    ", as.numeric(sqrt(z_test_computed$statistic)), "\n")
```

Identical results, and now the chunk cannot go stale.

### Q3 Interp

X-squared = 0.011344 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.9152, z = 0.1065. Do not
reject H0.

A z of 0.107 means the observed difference is about one tenth of one standard
error. Under H0 you would see a gap this large or larger 92% of the time. The
confidence interval for the difference in proportions, printed in the output
above, runs from -0.0568 to +0.0634: it comfortably contains zero, and it also
tells you the data could not have detected a gap smaller than about 6
percentage points either way. That is a statement about the study's precision,
which is more informative than "not significant".

Say this carefully. We have **not** shown that income group is irrelevant to
joining the Paris Agreement. We have shown that with 55 and 126 countries at 96%
membership on both sides, there is no room for a difference to show up. Almost
everybody joined. The ceiling, not the income effect, is doing the work.

R also emits a warning: `Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect`. That is
real and worth reading. The chi-squared approximation wants an expected count of
at least 5 in every cell of the 2x2 table, and the non-signer cells hold only 2
and 5 observed countries. With counts that small the approximation is shaky.
`fisher.test()` computes the exact answer for a table this size and is the right
tool when a cell is thin:

```{r fisher-check}
# Build the 2x2 contingency table the test works on:
#   row 1 = high income, row 2 = not high income
#   col 1 = signed, col 2 = did not sign
paris_table <- matrix(
  c(53, 55 - 53,
    121, 126 - 121),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(income = c("High income", "Not high income"),
                  paris  = c("Signed", "Did not sign"))
)
paris_table

fisher.test(paris_table)
```

Fisher's exact test gives p = 1, and its odds-ratio interval spans 1 by a wide
margin. Same conclusion as `prop.test()`, arrived at without the approximation,
and without the warning.





# 6. 2-Tail Means Comparison: Do high-income countries make higher or lower absolute emission reductions?

So if High Income countries are more likely to sign onto climate agreements than Mid/Low-Income countries, how do they behave after signing?

We're going to analyze this question by taking the mean emission reduction done by High Income countries and compare it with that of other countries. Since we don't have a strong reason to assume it will be one or the other, we will use a two-tailed test.

Our reductions will come from the `rel_reduction____` variables. The "rel" part marks these as "relative" emissions. This actually means two things!

1. The reductions are *relative* to their levels at the start of the agreement coming into force. 1 is Kyoto, 2 is Copenhagen, 3 is Paris.

2. The reductions are proportional: pledging `23.4` emissions reductions means to promise to decrease by 23.4%.

Sign convention, because it decides how every number below reads. In this file
`rel_reduction_low3` is stored so that a *positive* value is a pledged
reduction and a *negative* value is a pledged increase. Latvia's -472 is not a
472% cut; it is an implied 472% rise relative to its baseline, which is what
makes it an outlier rather than a hero.



### Many ways to skin a cat

When we ask, "Do high-income countries make higher or lower absolute emission reductions?", what exactly do we mean?

There are *many* ways to turn that question into a series of commands in R. Each of the 3 climate agreements has 2 reduction pledges; a high and a low value. This gives us 6 variables we can come up with a test on:

- we might average all of them
- we might average the high, or low, ones
- we might take just the most recent Paris Agreeement value

Any of these *could* be reasonable. We could even transform the data into proportional or absolute values. Now, what if we had an agenda to push?

- we might want to say rich countries aren't pulling their share in emissions reductions!
- we might want to say they **are** pulling their weight and everyone else should stop complaining!

If you're somehow committed to a specific result, you may be tempted to run a number of these, and report the result most favorable to your views. Or, run just the one you think will give the most convenient result and not explore any others.

"Researcher degrees of freedom" refers to this flexibility in how statistical analyses are designed and reported, and plays a major role in the Replication Crisis affecting much of academic social science. Economics is less badly affected than the worst offenders (psychology, sociology), but it's still a serious concern.

Put a number on it. Six outcome variables, times two income splits, times three
choices about outliers, times two tail choices, is 72 tests. If every one of
them were pure noise, the chance that at least one comes back significant at 5%
is about 97%. Reporting only that one is not fraud in the ordinary sense; each
step feels defensible on its own. That is exactly why it is the hard problem.

The defenses are procedural, not statistical: fix the specification before you
look at the outcome, say what you fixed, and report the tests you ran and not
only the ones that worked. Where a set of tests genuinely has to be run
together, adjust for it. `p.adjust()` in base R implements Bonferroni and
Benjamini-Hochberg corrections, and section 7's `TukeyHSD()` is the same idea
applied to all pairs of groups.


### Our specification and why

We will be taking the most recent pledge round, the Paris Agreement, and using the low versions. Why?

1. This uses pledges currently in place. We will suggest that climate change is being taken more seriously as of late, due to the rise in heat waves and changing weather patterns resulting from it.

2. We will use the `low` value to be cynical about countries' pledges. If rich countries really are shirking, we'd see it in their lower-bound pledges.

That reasoning is stated before the data are touched, and it is stated in public.
Both properties are what make it a specification rather than a rationalization.

### Our Hypotheses

- H0: High and non-High Income countries are not making different reduction pledges in the Paris Agreement.
- H1: High countries are making significantly greater or smaller reduction pledges in the Paris Agreement.

```{r}
# creating hypothsis 4 dataframe
hypothesis_4_df <- policy_df %>%
  select(country, Incomegroup, rel_reduction_low3)

print(hypothesis_4_df)
```



```{r}
# drop na values
hypothesis_4_df <- hypothesis_4_df %>%
  drop_na()

# taking first value of each country
hypothesis_4_df <- hypothesis_4_df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup()

# high and not high income split
hypothesis_4_hi_df <- hypothesis_4_df %>%
  filter(Incomegroup == "High income")

hypothesis_4_not_hi_df <- hypothesis_4_df %>%
  filter(Incomegroup != "High income")

```

Three details in that chunk.

`slice(1)` keeps the first *row* of each group, where the `summarise(first(...))`
pattern from earlier kept the first *value* of one column. The difference is
that `slice()` retains every column, which is what we need here because we still
want `Incomegroup` afterwards. Both are equally exposed to the same assumption:
that the value does not vary within a country.

`ungroup()` removes the grouping label that `group_by()` attached. Forgetting it
is a classic source of confusion, because subsequent `mutate()` or `summarise()`
calls would keep operating group by group and produce results you did not ask
for. Make a habit of ungrouping as soon as the grouped operation is finished.

The row counts: 10388 down to 7350 after `drop_na()`, which removes rows missing
`rel_reduction_low3` (2891 of them) or `Incomegroup` (686), with some overlap
between the two. Then down to 150 rows after `slice(1)`, one per country. Of
those, 52 are high income and 98 are not. This is a much smaller sample than
section 5's 181, on the same underlying data, because a country can be a party
to Paris without a numeric pledge recorded here.


As we remember from yesterday, Latvia's value was *quite* the outlier among the rich countries, as was Kiribati's in the non-rich countries.

Before the plot, one warning about how it is constructed. There is no meaningful
x variable for these two charts. The author builds an index `1, 2, 3, ...` purely
to spread the points out horizontally so they do not overlap. The horizontal
position of a point carries no information: it is just that country's position
in the sorted-by-name data frame. Only the vertical position means anything.

`seq_len(n)` generates `1, 2, ..., n`. Writing it as `seq_len(nrow(df))` rather
than a hard-coded `seq(1, 51)` means the length automatically tracks the data,
so an upstream change cannot leave the x and y vectors mismatched.


```{r}

# Make Latvia dataframe
latvia_df <- hypothesis_4_hi_df %>%
  filter(country == "Latvia")

# Make no-Latvia dataframe
hypothesis_4_hi_nolatvia_df <- hypothesis_4_hi_df %>%
  filter(country != "Latvia")

# Make x range, get y values
# seq_len(nrow(...)) is 1:51 here, and stays correct if the data changes.
x <- seq_len(nrow(hypothesis_4_hi_nolatvia_df))
y <- hypothesis_4_hi_nolatvia_df$rel_reduction_low3

# Create scatter plot
plot <- ggplot(data = hypothesis_4_hi_nolatvia_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  # A second geom_point layer with its own data: one red dot for Latvia,
  # placed at x = 25 (mid-plot) and at Latvia's actual y value.
  geom_point(data = latvia_df, aes(x = 25, y = rel_reduction_low3), color = "red", shape = 19) +
  geom_text(data = latvia_df, aes(x = 25, y = rel_reduction_low3 + 15, label = "Latvia"), vjust = 0) +

  # Axis labels
  labs(y = "Paris Agreement Emission Reduction Pledges") +

  # Added: the x axis is an arbitrary index, and saying so on the plot avoids
  # readers inventing a meaning for it.
  labs(x = "Country index (no meaning, spacing only)") +

  # Plot title
  labs(title = "What the Hell, Latvia?")

print(plot)
```

Every high-income country except Latvia sits in a band between about -130 and
+85. Latvia, the red point, is at -472. It is roughly three and a half times
further from the pack than the next most extreme value, and it drags the
high-income mean from +9.2 down to -0.04 on its own. One country out of 52
moving the group average by 9 units is the definition of an influential
observation.

Repeated `labs()` calls are fine, by the way. Each one adds to the label set
rather than replacing it, so the three calls above could equally be written as
one `labs(x = ..., y = ..., title = ...)`.

For Kiribati's case:

```{r}
# Make x range, get y values, and labels
x <- seq_len(nrow(hypothesis_4_not_hi_df))
y <- hypothesis_4_not_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3
labels <- hypothesis_4_not_hi_df$country

# Create scatter plot
plot <- ggplot(data = hypothesis_4_not_hi_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = labels), vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0.5, size = 3) +

  # Axis labels
  labs(y = "Paris Agreement Emission Reduction Pledges") +
  labs(x = "Country index (no meaning, spacing only)") +

  # Plot title
  labs(title = "Non-High Income Paris Pledges")

print(plot)
```

This plot is dominated by a single point at -86,515: Kiribati. Everything else
is compressed into a flat line near zero, and the 98 country labels overlap into
an unreadable smear along it. Both problems are worth seeing rather than fixing,
because they are what an outlier of this magnitude does to a chart. Kiribati's
value is roughly 180 times Latvia's and 300 times the next largest non-high-income
value, which is Madagascar at -280.

A cleaner version of the same data, with the extreme values excluded and the
labels dropped:

```{r pledges-clean-plot}
# Combine the two groups into one tibble with a group label, so ggplot can
# color by it. bind_rows() stacks data frames vertically.
pledges_long <- bind_rows(
  hypothesis_4_hi_df     %>% mutate(group = "High income"),
  hypothesis_4_not_hi_df %>% mutate(group = "Not high income")
) %>%
  filter(!country %in% c("Latvia", "Kiribati", "Madagascar"))

# %in% tests membership in a vector; ! negates it. So this keeps every country
# that is not one of the three named outliers.

ggplot(pledges_long, aes(x = group, y = rel_reduction_low3, fill = group)) +
  # A boxplot shows the median (thick line), the middle 50% of values (box),
  # and the reach of the non-outlying values (whiskers).
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.4, outlier.shape = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  # Jitter nudges points sideways at random so overlapping values stay visible.
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Paris pledges overlap almost completely across income groups",
    subtitle = "Latvia, Kiribati and Madagascar removed; 51 and 96 countries",
    x = "Income group",
    y = "Paris Agreement pledged reduction, low bound (percent)"
  )
```

The two boxes overlap over nearly their whole range. High-income countries have
a higher median (13.7 against 0.0) and a mean of 9.2 against -1.3, but the
not-high-income group is far more dispersed: its standard deviation is 60.3
against 28.7, and it holds both the largest cut (+340) and the largest implied
increase (-200) in the trimmed data. The dashed line at zero separates pledged
cuts from pledged increases; both groups have members on both sides. A visible
difference in center combined with heavy overlap and unequal spread is exactly
the configuration that produces a non-significant t-test, which is what happens
below.

We'll run the same two hypothesis tests comparing the two reductions, with and without outliers.

### Q4 Hypothesis Testing

```{r}
mean(hypothesis_4_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3) # same mean value as in python
var(hypothesis_4_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3) # same variance as in python

mean(hypothesis_4_not_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3) # same value as in python
var(hypothesis_4_not_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3) # again same value
```

`var()` is the variance, the squared standard deviation. Read these four numbers
together before running any test.

The high-income mean is -0.037 with a variance of 5267, so a standard deviation
of about 73. The not-high-income mean is -887 with a variance of 76,373,436, so
a standard deviation of about 8739. The second group's spread is 120 times the
first group's. Both figures are entirely driven by the outliers just plotted:
Kiribati alone accounts for essentially all of that variance.

This is the situation Welch's t-test exists for. R's `t.test()` defaults to
Welch, which does not assume the two groups share a variance and adjusts the
degrees of freedom downward instead. That is why the df below comes out as
97.03 rather than a whole number.

T-test:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?t.test
```

Unlike in Python, where we used a new function, we can get by just with the same `t.test()` function in R.

We do add a second data vector, however. Now we use both `x` and `y`.

The null hypothesis changes shape when you supply two samples. With one sample
and `mu`, H0 was "this mean equals that fixed number". With `x` and `y`, H0 is
"these two population means are equal", and `mu` defaults to 0, meaning a zero
difference. R keeps the same function name and infers which test you want from
which arguments you supply.

```{r}
# Two-sample t-test
t_test_result <- t.test(x = hypothesis_4_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3, y = hypothesis_4_not_hi_df$rel_reduction_low3, alternative = "two.sided")

# Output results
cat("T-statistic:", t_test_result$statistic, "\n")
cat("P-value:", t_test_result$p.value, "\n")
```

t = 1.0046, p = 0.3176, on 97.03 degrees of freedom. Under H0 you would see a
gap this large or larger about 32% of the time, so do not reject.

The estimated difference in means is about 887 percentage points, which is
enormous, and the test still finds nothing. That combination is the lesson of
this chunk. The difference is enormous because Kiribati is in the sample, and
the standard error is even more enormous for the same reason. When one
observation drives both the estimate and its uncertainty, the test has nothing
to work with.

Based on this result, we would conclude that High and not-High Income countries are not making (statistically) significantly different reduction pledges.

But we saw that Latvia and Kiribati are extreme outliers. The paper mentioned Madagascar as well. What if we remove them?

Removing outliers is a researcher degree of freedom of exactly the kind
described above, so state the rule and show both results. That is what the next
chunk does: it prints the trimmed test *alongside* the full-sample test rather
than replacing it.

```{r}
# Make high income df without Latvia
hypothesis_4_hi_no_latvia_df <- hypothesis_4_hi_df %>%
  filter(country != "Latvia")

# Make not high income df without Kiribati and Madagascar
hypothesis_4_not_hi_no_kiri_mad_df <- hypothesis_4_not_hi_df %>%
  filter(country != "Kiribati" & country != "Madagascar")

# Two-sample t-test
t_test_result <- t.test(hypothesis_4_hi_no_latvia_df$rel_reduction_low3, hypothesis_4_not_hi_no_kiri_mad_df$rel_reduction_low3)

# Output results
cat("T-statistic:", t_test_result$statistic, "\n")
cat("P-value:", t_test_result$p.value, "\n")
```

`&` is logical AND, applied element by element down the column, so the filter
keeps rows that are neither Kiribati nor Madagascar. `|` is OR and `!` is NOT.
Note that `country != "Kiribati" & country != "Madagascar"` is the same as
`!country %in% c("Kiribati", "Madagascar")`, which scales better once the list
grows past two.

t = 1.4313, p = 0.1545, on 143.67 degrees of freedom. Still not significant at
5%, but the picture underneath has changed completely:

| Sample | n (HI) | n (other) | mean HI | mean other | t | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All countries | 52 | 98 | -0.04 | -886.93 | 1.005 | 0.318 |
| Outliers removed | 51 | 96 | 9.22 | -1.29 | 1.431 | 0.155 |

Removing three countries out of 150 flips the sign of the estimated gap from
strongly negative to positive, and moves the difference in means from 887 to
10.5. The p-value barely moves because both the numerator and the denominator
of the t-statistic collapse together. Notice also that the degrees of freedom
jump from 97 to 144: with the variances now comparable, Welch's adjustment costs
much less.

The honest summary of section 6 is that the data cannot answer the question. The
result is not significant either way, and the point estimate is not stable to
dropping three observations out of 150.



```{r}
# extract data series

data_series1 <- hypothesis_4_hi_no_latvia_df$rel_reduction_low3
data_series2 <- hypothesis_4_not_hi_no_kiri_mad_df$rel_reduction_low3

length(data_series1)
length(seq(1,51))

# Create a data frame for plotting
plot_data <- data.frame(
  # seq_along(v) is seq_len(length(v)): 1..51 and 1..96 here. Deriving the index
  # from the data means the x and y vectors cannot fall out of sync.
  x = c(seq_along(data_series1), seq_along(data_series2)),
  y = c(data_series1, data_series2),
  # rep() repeats the first vector's elements the number of times given in the
  # second, producing 51 "High Income" labels then 96 "Not High Income" ones.
  group = rep(c("High Income", "Not High Income"), c(length(data_series1), length(data_series2)))
)

# Create the scatter plot
plot <- ggplot(data = plot_data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = group)) +
  geom_point() +

  # Add labels and legend
  labs(y = "Paris Agreement Reduction Pledges", x= "X-axis just to separate plot values", color = "Group") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red"), labels = c("High Income", "Not High Income")) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Group")) +

  # Add a title
  labs(title = "Scatter Plot of rel_reduction_low3, Outliers Removed")

# Show the plot
print(plot)
```

The two `length()` calls are a sanity check: both print 51, confirming the index
and the data agree in length. `c()` here is doing the stacking, gluing the two
groups' values into one long vector, with `rep()` building a matching label
vector so `ggplot` knows which point came from which group.

`data.frame()` is base R's constructor, the plain equivalent of `tibble()` used
earlier. `scale_color_manual()` overrides the default palette with named colors;
`guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Group"))` sets the legend title, which
`labs(color = "Group")` on the line above has already done, so it is redundant
but harmless.

We can get an intuitive feeling for this result with the above scatter plot. Ignore the horizontal variance - it's just to separate out the plot points. On the vertical axis defining reduction pledges, we can see that High Income and other countries aren't distributed differently.

When we plot *with* the outliers, we see Kiribati's value down around -86,500, and then all others clumped together as a solid mass, which provides some justification for removing the outliers.

Compare this scatter with the boxplot drawn a few chunks up. They show the same
147 countries. The scatter makes the individual extremes visible, in particular
the red point near +340 and the one near -200, both non-high-income. The boxplot
makes the centers and the quartiles comparable at a glance. Neither is better;
use the scatter when the individual observations matter and the boxplot when the
comparison of distributions matters.


# 7. Group Comparisons: Are average emission levels different by region?

So, if High Income countries aren't making bigger or smaller reductions than others, what does overall emission variability look like?

We'll look at actual emissions, on a per-capita basis, this time. Groups will be made by overall world region. Because these vary over time, we can't just take any entry in a country's data. Instead, we'll remove all NaN values and then take the most recent value.

Sections 3 to 6 all compared at most two groups. Here there are seven, and that
changes the tool. Running a t-test on every pair would mean 21 tests, and at 5%
each you would expect about one false positive by chance alone even if all seven
regions were identical.

The **ANOVA** (analysis of variance) sidesteps that with a single test of a
single null: all seven group means are equal. It works by splitting the total
variation in `GHG_percapita` into two parts, between groups and within groups,
and comparing them:

```
F = (variation between group means) / (variation within groups)
```

If the regions really are alike, the between-group piece is just sampling noise
of the same size as the within-group piece and F sits near 1. If the regions
differ, the numerator grows and F rises. The **F distribution** gives the
p-value, and it has two degrees of freedom numbers rather than one: 6 for the
numerator (7 groups minus 1) and 201 for the denominator (208 observations minus
7 groups).

What the ANOVA does not tell you is *which* regions differ. That takes a
follow-up, which is what `TukeyHSD()` provides at the end of this section.

### Hypotheses

- H0: Mean per-capita emissions are equal across world regions
- H1: Mean per-capita emissions are not equal across world regions

Read H1 precisely: it says *at least one* region differs from at least one
other. Rejecting H0 does not say all seven differ, and it does not name a
culprit.

### Steps

We'll get a dataframe with the `country`, `year`, `wbregion` and `GHG_percapita` variables, remove NaN values and grab the most recent year. Then, we'll compare the average `GHG_percapita` values by region.


```{r}
# Assign hypothesis 5 dataframe
hypothesis_5_df <- policy_df %>%
  select(country, year, wbregion, GHG_percapita)

# Drop NaN values
hypothesis_5_df <- hypothesis_5_df %>%
  drop_na()

# group by country, get most recent year for each
hypothesis_5_df <- hypothesis_5_df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  filter(year == max(year)) %>%
  ungroup()

print(hypothesis_5_df)
```

The middle step is the one to study. `filter()` inside `group_by()` evaluates
its condition separately within each group, so `year == max(year)` means "the
maximum year *for this country*", not the maximum across the whole file. That is
grouped filtering, and it is a distinct move from grouped summarizing: it keeps
whole rows rather than collapsing them.

Why the most recent year instead of a country average, as in section 4? Because
the question is about emission *levels* now, not about a country's typical level
over five decades. Averaging 1970 to 2015 would blend eras with very different
energy systems.

The result is 208 rows, one per country, and every one of them is from 2015.
That uniformity is convenient but not guaranteed by the code: if one country's
data ended in 2009, `max(year)` would return 2009 for it and the comparison
would mix years. Check it rather than assume it, which is what the next chunk
does for the regions.

Quick check of what the world regions are:

```{r}
# Get unique regions
unique_regions <- unique(hypothesis_5_df$wbregion)

# Print the unique regions
print(unique_regions)
```

So, they're regions, not continents.

`unique()` returns each distinct value once, in order of first appearance. Seven
World Bank regions survive the cleaning. Their sizes are very unequal, which
matters for what follows:

```{r region-counts}
# n() counts rows in the current group. Sorting by the mean makes the ordering
# in the plot below easy to anticipate.
region_summary <- hypothesis_5_df %>%
  group_by(wbregion) %>%
  summarise(
    n_countries = n(),
    mean_GHG    = mean(GHG_percapita),
    median_GHG  = median(GHG_percapita),
    sd_GHG      = sd(GHG_percapita)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_GHG))   # desc() sorts largest first

region_summary
```

North America has 4 countries and Europe & Central Asia has 50. A mean computed
from 4 observations is a much shakier number than one computed from 50, and the
confidence intervals in the Tukey output at the end of this section will reflect
that: the North America comparisons have by far the widest intervals.

```{r region-boxplot}
# reorder(wbregion, GHG_percapita, FUN = median) sorts the regions by their
# median so the boxes climb rather than sitting in alphabetical order.
ggplot(hypothesis_5_df,
       aes(x = reorder(wbregion, GHG_percapita, FUN = median), y = GHG_percapita)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85", outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.55, color = "steelblue", size = 1.6) +
  # stat_summary computes something per group and draws it: here the mean,
  # as a red diamond (shape 18), on top of the median line of the boxplot.
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 3.5, color = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Per-capita emissions by World Bank region, 2015",
    subtitle = "Boxes show median and quartiles; red diamonds are group means; 208 countries",
    x = "World Bank region",
    y = "GHG per capita (2015)"
  )
```

This is the ANOVA in picture form. Two features drive the result.

The centers are not level. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia have medians of
1.57 and 1.93, while North America's is 16.6 and Europe & Central Asia's is
8.08. That vertical separation is the between-group variation in the F ratio's
numerator.

But the within-region spread is large and very uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa is
tightly packed near zero with a handful of stragglers, and its standard
deviation is 5.82; the Middle East & North Africa box is the widest of the seven
at sd 16.0, reaching out to Qatar at 66.1, the highest value in the data. That
spread is the denominator, and it is why F comes out at 4.5 rather than
something much larger.

Note also that the red mean diamonds and the black median lines disagree
substantially in several regions. Six of the seven means sit to the right of
their median, the signature of right-skew; the Middle East & North Africa gap is
the widest, mean 13.8 against median 6.30. Only North America, with four
countries, has a mean below its median. ANOVA tests means. With skewed groups, a
test of means and a test of medians can reach different conclusions.


### Q5 Hypothesis Testing

`aov()` is our F-test, like in Python. Its setup is different, but the outcome is the same.

First, we input a formula, with our dependent variable (i.e. which one we want to test), with a tilde (~) connecting it with the variable that splits it into groups.

This looks like `GHG_percapita ~ wbregion`

In comparison, our Python equivalent involved us filtering the different samples ourselves and then inputting them separately.

We also use a `data` argument, which states where to get the `formula` variables from.

Then, we call `summary()` around our anova variable, and can extract the F-statistic and P-value.

The **formula** is worth a paragraph, because it is R's single most distinctive
piece of syntax and it recurs in `lm()`, `glm()` and most modelling functions.
A formula is written `outcome ~ predictors` and is read "outcome modelled by
predictors". It is not evaluated where you write it. It is an unevaluated
description of a relationship that the modelling function then interprets, which
is why you can write bare column names with no quotes and no `$`.

Because `wbregion` is on the right of the tilde and is a character column,
`aov()` converts it to a factor and treats its seven distinct values as seven
groups. Had it been numeric, `aov()` would have fitted a straight line through
it instead, which is a completely different model. That silent difference is the
main reason to know what a factor is.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?aov
```



```{r}
# Perform ANOVA test
anova_result <- aov(GHG_percapita ~ wbregion, data = hypothesis_5_df)

# Get ANOVA summary
summary_result <- summary(anova_result)

# Extract F-statistic and p-value
f_statistic <- summary_result[[1]]$F[1]
p_value <- summary_result[[1]]$"Pr(>F)"[1]

# Output the results
cat("F-statistic:", f_statistic, "\n")
cat("P-value:", p_value, "\n")
```

The extraction line deserves unpacking. `summary()` on an `aov` object returns a
list containing one data frame. `summary_result[[1]]` reaches into the list and
pulls out that data frame; double brackets get the element itself, where single
brackets `[1]` would return a one-element list still wrapped up. Then `$F` is
the F column and `[1]` is its first entry, the row for `wbregion`. `"Pr(>F)"` is
quoted because the name contains characters that are not legal in a bare R name.

The full table is more informative than the two extracted numbers:

```{r anova-table}
summary_result
```

Read it column by column. `Df` 6 and 201 are the two degrees of freedom.
`Sum Sq` splits the total variation: 2491 lies between the regional means and
18353 lies within regions, so region accounts for 2491 / (2491 + 18353) = 12% of
the variation in per-capita emissions. `Mean Sq` is `Sum Sq / Df`: 415.2 and
91.3. `F value` is the ratio of those two, 415.2 / 91.3 = 4.547. The stars are
R's significance codes, with three meaning p < 0.001.

The high F-Stat leads to a very low P-value, and so we can reject the null hypothesis that the regions have equal per-capita emissions values.

To be exact: F = 4.547 on 6 and 201 degrees of freedom, p = 0.000239. If all
seven regions had the same mean, an F this large would appear about 2 times in
10,000. Reject H0.

Keep the effect size in view alongside that. Region explains 12% of the
variation between countries; the other 88% is differences between countries
within the same region. "Statistically significant" and "most of the story" are
different claims.
