Extending this a bit, we can run a Tukey test, which analyzes each pair and reports a p-value for if the groups differ.

Tukey's Honest Significant Differences runs all 21 pairwise comparisons but
widens each interval so that the *family-wide* error rate stays at 5%. That is,
the probability of at least one false positive across all 21 comparisons is 5%,
not 5% per comparison. This is why the `p adj` column can be much larger than
the p-value an ordinary t-test on the same pair would give: it is paying for the
multiplicity. It is the same guard against researcher degrees of freedom that
section 6 discussed, built into the procedure.

```{r}
# Tukey Honest Significant Differences on the fitted ANOVA
tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(anova_result)

print(tukey_result)
```

Each row is one pair, named `A-B`. `diff` is mean(A) minus mean(B). `lwr` and
`upr` bound a 95% family-wise confidence interval for that difference, and
`p adj` is the adjusted p-value. The decision rule: the pair differs
significantly if the interval excludes zero, equivalently if `p adj` < 0.05.

Twenty-one rows of numbers are hard to scan, so plot them.

```{r tukey-plot}
# TukeyHSD returns a list; $wbregion is a matrix. Convert to a data frame and
# move the pair names out of the row names into a real column, because ggplot
# cannot map row names to anything.
tukey_df <- as.data.frame(tukey_result$wbregion) %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "pair")

# The matrix column is literally named "p adj", with a space, so backticks are
# needed to refer to it. Renaming it avoids that for the rest of the chunk.
tukey_df <- tukey_df %>%
  rename(p_adj = `p adj`) %>%
  mutate(significant = if_else(p_adj < 0.05, "p adj < 0.05", "not significant"))

ggplot(tukey_df, aes(x = diff, y = reorder(pair, diff), color = significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  # geom_linerange draws the interval; supplying xmin/xmax makes it horizontal.
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("p adj < 0.05" = "firebrick",
                                "not significant" = "grey45")) +
  labs(
    title = "Tukey pairwise comparisons of regional per-capita emissions",
    subtitle = "Family-wise 95% intervals; a pair differs only if its interval clears zero",
    x = "Difference in mean GHG per capita (tonnes)",
    y = "Region pair",
    color = NULL
  )
```

Read the chart against the dashed zero line. Nineteen of the 21 intervals cross
it and are drawn in grey: those pairs are not distinguishable. Two clear it,
both involving Sub-Saharan Africa, and they are red.

Notice how wide the intervals are for any pair involving North America. That is
the n = 4 problem made visible. All six of the widest intervals in the chart
involve North America, and the two largest gaps in the whole table are its
comparisons with South Asia (-13.69) and Sub-Saharan Africa (-12.54). Neither is
significant, because four countries cannot pin the mean down: the South Asia
comparison has an interval 34.9 units wide, against 15.1 for the significant
Sub-Saharan Africa versus Middle East & North Africa pair, whose gap is smaller
at -10.69.

For reference, the group means themselves:

```{r}
# Calculate average GHG_percapita values for each wbregion
avg_per_region <- hypothesis_5_df %>%
  group_by(wbregion) %>%
  summarize(average_GHG = mean(GHG_percapita, na.rm = TRUE))

# Print the result
print(avg_per_region)
```

`na.rm = TRUE` tells `mean()` to drop missing values before computing rather
than returning `NA`. It does nothing here, since `drop_na()` already removed
them, but it is a sensible habit when you are not certain.


Interestingly, it only registers Sub-Saharan Africa/Europe & Central Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa/Middle East & North Africa as having statistically significant differences.

The two significant pairs and their adjusted p-values:

- Sub-Saharan Africa vs Middle East & North Africa: difference -10.69, interval
  [-18.22, -3.16], p adj = 0.00070
- Sub-Saharan Africa vs Europe & Central Asia: difference -6.12, interval
  [-11.81, -0.43], p adj = 0.0260

The near miss is South Asia vs Middle East & North Africa at p adj = 0.0523,
which would have been significant on an unadjusted test. That is the correction
doing its job, and it is also a reminder that 0.05 is a convention rather than a
threshold with any physical meaning.

Why so few? Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest mean (3.08) and 50 countries, so
its comparisons combine large gaps with tight standard errors. The two regions with the highest means are both small: North America with 4
countries, the smallest of the seven, and Middle East & North Africa with 20,
the third smallest and the one with the largest internal spread of any region
(sd 16.0). Only South Asia, with 8, sits between them on size. Their intervals are consequently too wide to exclude zero
against anything but Sub-Saharan Africa, and in North America's case against
nothing at all. The overall ANOVA can detect that *something* differs while
Tukey, paying for 21 comparisons at once, can pin down only the two clearest
cases.




# 8. Regression: Is there evidence for an Environmental Kuznets Curve?

Much of our analysis has related to the relationship of emissions, or emission pledges, to national wealth. The following model will finish off our investigation.

The "Environmental Kuznets Curve" relates environmental quality with economic growth. It suggests that as a country becomes wealthier, it will first see degraded environmental quality, likely as a result of growing energy and land use in manufacturing industries. However, beyond a certain point, further increases to per-capita income will cause the environment to improve again. From here on, marginal willingness to pay for environmental quality exceeds the marginal damage caused by economic growth (or said economic growth becomes more energy efficient, or the services sector comes to dominate manufacturing).

We will model this by regressing per-capita greenhouse gas emissions against GDP/capita, and (GDP/capita)^2. The first GDP/Capita term provides the initial environmental degradation as industry grows. The quadratic term, if theory holds, will be negative and eventually dominate the linear term.

Everything so far compared group averages. **Regression** does something
different: it estimates how an outcome changes as a predictor changes,
continuously, and reports a coefficient with its own standard error and
p-value. The hypothesis-testing machinery is identical; only the estimand
changes.

Ordinary least squares picks the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared
vertical distances between the observed points and the fitted line. Each
coefficient answers "how much does the outcome move per one-unit move in this
predictor, holding the other predictors fixed", and each comes with a t-test of
the null that it is zero.

Why a squared term. A model with GDP alone can only produce a straight line: as
income rises, emissions rise forever, or fall forever. Adding `GDP^2` lets the
fitted curve bend. The two coefficients together define a parabola. If b1 is
positive and b2 is negative you get the inverted U the theory predicts, peaking
at GDP = -b1 / (2 * b2). That turning point is the number to compute, and it is
the number this section ends on.

### Hypotheses
H0: There is no evidence of per-capita emissions falling with increasing wealth levels
H1: A negative coefficient on the (GDP/capita)^2 term provides evidence of falling per-capita emissions with high wealth level

A negative squared coefficient is necessary for the Kuznets story but not
sufficient. The turning point also has to fall inside the range of GDP we
actually observe. A curve that peaks at an income level no country has ever
reached is, over the observed data, indistinguishable from a straight line
sloping up. Hold that thought.

### Steps

We will make a dataset with country, year, GHG_percapita, and GDP_percapita variables. Then, we drop all missing values, calculate the squared GDP per capita variable, and run our regression.

```{r}
# Initialize regression dataframe
regression_df <- policy_df %>%
  select(country, year, GHG_percapita, GDP_percapita)

# Drop missing values
regression_df <- regression_df %>%
  drop_na()

# Calculate GDP_percapita_square
regression_df$GDP_percapita_square <- regression_df$GDP_percapita^2

# Print the first few rows of the dataframe
head(regression_df)
```

Note the two styles of adding a column sitting side by side in this document.
Section 3 used `mutate(total_pledges = ...)`; this chunk uses
`regression_df$GDP_percapita_square <- ...`. Both work. Base R assignment with
`$` is fine for a one-off; `mutate()` chains into a pipeline and reads better
when several columns are created at once. Pick one per script and stay with it.

Unlike every previous section, there is no collapsing to one row per country.
The regression uses all 7436 country-year observations from 190 countries,
1970 to 2015. That is a deliberate choice, since the relationship between income
and emissions is meant to hold within a country over time as well as across
countries. It also means the observations are not independent: Canada's 2014 and
2015 rows are nearly the same country in nearly the same state. The classical
standard errors printed below take no account of that, and they will be too
small as a result. This is one of the two reasons the robust standard errors at
the end of the section matter.


First, it's never a bad idea to visualize our data. As we saw a few hypotheses back, it helps you catch outliers, and see any abnormal patterns in your data.

```{r}
# Create logged variables
log_gdppc <- log(regression_df$GDP_percapita)
log_ghgpc <- log(regression_df$GHG_percapita)

# Create a scatter plot
plot <- ggplot(data = data.frame(log_gdppc, log_ghgpc), aes(x = log_gdppc, y = log_ghgpc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  # Axis labels corrected: both variables on this plot are logged.
  labs(x = "log(GDP per capita)", y = "log(GHG per capita)") +
  ggtitle("Scatter Plot of log GDP per Capita vs. log GHG per Capita") +

  # Add linear regression line
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE)

print(plot)
```

`log()` in R is the natural logarithm, base e, not base 10; that is `log10()`.
Logging both axes is standard for variables that span orders of magnitude, as
these do: GDP per capita runs from 162 to 116,233 and GHG per capita from 0.41
to 323. It is safe here only because both variables are strictly positive, which
was checked. `log(0)` is `-Inf` and `log(-1)` is `NaN` with a warning.

`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` fits a straight line by least squares and draws it.
`se = FALSE` suppresses the shaded confidence band; `alpha = 0.4` makes the
points partly transparent so that dense regions render darker, which is
essential with 7436 overlapping points.

Working with logarithm values, the relationship is... iffy. However, the logarithms make this already a nonlinear relationship, compressing in the very high values. What if we use raw data?

What the plot actually shows, to put a number on "iffy": the correlation between
the two logged variables is 0.76, and a simple log-log regression gives a slope
of 0.55 with an R-squared of 0.58. So the association is strong and clearly
upward, and the cloud is wide. Reading it as an elasticity, a 10% rise in income
comes with a 5.5% rise in per-capita emissions on average. There is no visible
downturn at the right-hand end, which is the first piece of evidence against the
Kuznets story.

```{r}
# Create variables
gdppc <- regression_df$GDP_percapita
ghgpc <- regression_df$GHG_percapita

# Create a scatter plot
plot <- ggplot(data = data.frame(gdppc, ghgpc), aes(x = gdppc, y = ghgpc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita", y = "GHG per Capita") +
  ggtitle("Scatter Plot of GDP per Capita vs. GHG per Capita") +

  # Add quadratic regression line
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), color = "red", se = FALSE)

print(plot)
```

`formula = y ~ poly(x, 2)` tells `geom_smooth` to fit a second-degree polynomial
rather than a straight line, so the drawn curve matches the model specification
we are about to estimate. `poly()` builds orthogonal polynomial terms; the fitted
values are the same as from `x + x^2`, though the individual coefficients are
scaled differently.

Using non-logged, raw values, is rough. The data is blown way, way up by the extreme outliers on `GHG_percapita`.

*However*, the greenhouse gas emissions per capita flattens out remarkably past ~25, with even some of the richest countries being only marginally higher than the poorest. The outliers may be problematic for our regression, but we can give it a try, in `reg_1`, using non-logged values.

Reading the plot carefully: the vertical axis reaches past 300 because a handful
of country-years have per-capita emissions above 60, but fewer than 1% do, so
almost the entire cloud is squashed into the bottom tenth of the panel. The
fitted red curve rises across the whole plotted range, with only slight bending
near the right edge. The flattening the author describes is in the *scatter* at
high emission levels, not in the fitted curve, and the points out at
GDP per capita above 100,000 (0.2% of the sample) are what pull the right end of
the curve around.

That difference between the cloud and the curve is exactly what the coefficients
below quantify.


### Running Regression

The `lm()` function is our equivalent to the `sm.OLS()` function we used in Python.

Its arguments are similar to `aov()`.

- `formula`: specifies the outcome variable (y) and the explanatory variables (x1, x2, etc), like `y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 (...)`
- `data`: specifies the dataframe to take `y`, `x1`, `x2`, etc, from

We then run `summary()` to output our results. We first input the variable we assigned our regression to, and then our standard errors.

`type`: our standard errors. We use "HC3" heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors again

One difference from Python worth flagging. `sm.OLS()` in statsmodels requires
you to add a constant column yourself with `sm.add_constant()`. `lm()` includes
an intercept automatically. If you ever want to suppress it, write
`y ~ x - 1` or `y ~ x + 0`, but you almost never should.

Note also that `+` inside a formula does not mean addition. `y ~ x1 + x2` means
"include x1 and include x2 as separate predictors". Formula syntax has its own
grammar: `:` is an interaction, `*` is both main effects and their interaction,
and `I()` protects real arithmetic, so `I(x^2)` would compute the square inline
instead of creating the column beforehand as this section does.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?lm
```




```{r}
# Create linear regression model
reg_1 <- lm(GHG_percapita ~ GDP_percapita + GDP_percapita_square, data = regression_df)

# Print summary of the model
print(summary(reg_1))
```

Work through the output block by block.

**Residuals.** The five-number summary of the prediction errors. Median -1.58
against a maximum of +282 says the errors are wildly right-skewed: the model
under-predicts a small number of very high emitters by an enormous margin. That
is the first warning sign for the standard errors.

**Coefficients.** Four columns per row.

- `Estimate` is the fitted coefficient. The intercept is 2.992, so a country
  with zero GDP per capita is predicted to emit 3.0 tonnes per person, which is
  extrapolation outside the data and should not be interpreted. `GDP_percapita`
  is 4.265e-04, meaning one extra dollar of GDP per capita comes with 0.0004
  extra tonnes; multiply by 10,000 to get a usable statement, 4.3 extra tonnes
  per additional $10,000. `GDP_percapita_square` is -6.068e-10, negative as the
  theory predicts.
- `Std. Error` is the estimated standard deviation of the coefficient across
  repeated samples.
- `t value` is Estimate / Std. Error, testing H0 that the coefficient is zero.
  Same t-statistic as in sections 3 and 4, different quantity.
- `Pr(>|t|)` is the two-tailed p-value for that null.

The squared term has t = -2.052 and p = 0.0403. On classical standard errors,
it clears 5%. Hold that result until the next chunk.

**R-squared** is 0.2246: the model accounts for 22% of the variation in
per-capita emissions. The adjusted version, 0.2243, penalizes for the number of
predictors and is nearly identical here because 2 predictors against 7436
observations costs almost nothing.

**The F-statistic** at the bottom, 1076 on 2 and 7433 df, tests the joint null
that both slope coefficients are zero. It is the same F distribution as section
7's ANOVA, used for a different null.

```{r}
# Create linear regression model with robust standard errors
reg_robust <- lm(GHG_percapita ~ GDP_percapita + GDP_percapita_square, data = regression_df)

# Print summary of the model with robust standard errors
coeftest(reg_robust, vcov = vcovHC(reg_robust, type = "HC3"))
```

Our values come up mostly the same as yesterday, with differences only because of varying display methods in Python/R.

Note first that `reg_robust` is the identical model to `reg_1`: same formula,
same data, so the coefficient estimates are exactly the same. Robust standard
errors change the *uncertainty* attached to the coefficients, never the
coefficients themselves. The line could equally have been written
`coeftest(reg_1, vcov = vcovHC(reg_1, type = "HC3"))`.

What "robust" is protecting against is **heteroskedasticity**: error variance
that changes across the range of the predictors. Classical OLS standard errors
assume it is constant. The scatter plot above shows it plainly is not, since the
vertical spread of emissions grows with GDP. `vcovHC()` from `sandwich`
recomputes the variance matrix without that assumption, and `coeftest()` from
`lmtest` re-runs the t-tests using it. `"HC3"` is the small-sample-corrected
version and the sensible default.

Now compare the two coefficient tables, because this is the punchline of the
section:

| Term | Estimate | Classical SE | Classical p | HC3 SE | HC3 p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (Intercept) | 2.992 | 0.1906 | < 2e-16 | 0.2728 | < 2e-16 |
| GDP_percapita | 4.265e-04 | 2.010e-05 | < 2e-16 | 7.303e-05 | 5.4e-09 |
| GDP_percapita_square | -6.068e-10 | 2.958e-10 | 0.0403 | 1.558e-09 | 0.6969 |

The robust standard error on the squared term is 5.3 times the classical one,
and the p-value moves from 0.040 to 0.697. Significant becomes nowhere near
significant. The linear term survives comfortably either way.

The conclusion depends entirely on which standard error you believe, and here
the robust one is the more credible: the residuals are heavily skewed, the
variance visibly widens with GDP, and the panel structure means observations
within a country are correlated. So we do not reject H0. There is no reliable
evidence of the quadratic turn.

One more check settles it. Compute where the fitted parabola actually peaks:

```{r turning-point}
# coef() extracts the coefficient vector from a fitted model. Elements 2 and 3
# are the linear and quadratic terms. For y = b0 + b1*x + b2*x^2 the vertex is
# at x = -b1 / (2 * b2).
b <- coef(reg_1)
turning_point <- -b[2] / (2 * b[3])

cat("Fitted turning point, GDP per capita:", round(as.numeric(turning_point)), "\n")
cat("Highest GDP per capita observed:     ", round(max(regression_df$GDP_percapita)), "\n")
```

```{r regression-fit-plot}
# Build a grid of GDP values spanning the observed range, compute the squared
# term the same way the model expects, then predict() the fitted curve on it.
prediction_grid <- tibble(
  GDP_percapita = seq(min(regression_df$GDP_percapita),
                      max(regression_df$GDP_percapita),
                      length.out = 200)
) %>%
  mutate(GDP_percapita_square = GDP_percapita^2)

prediction_grid$fitted <- predict(reg_1, newdata = prediction_grid)

ggplot(regression_df, aes(x = GDP_percapita, y = GHG_percapita)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = prediction_grid, aes(x = GDP_percapita, y = fitted),
            color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.1) +
  # coord_cartesian zooms without discarding rows, so the fit is still computed
  # on all 7436 observations. Using ylim() instead would drop points and
  # silently refit anything drawn by geom_smooth.
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "The fitted Kuznets curve never turns over inside the data",
    subtitle = "7436 country-years, 1970-2015; vertical axis clipped at 60 for legibility",
    x = "GDP per capita (USD)",
    y = "GHG per capita (tonnes)"
  )
```

The fitted turning point is at GDP per capita of about 351,000 USD. The richest
observation in the data is 116,233 USD, three times smaller. The red curve in
the plot is the fitted model over the entire observed range, and it rises the
whole way, from 3.1 tonnes at the poorest observation to 44.4 at the richest,
bending only slightly at the top.

So the Kuznets result fails on all three counts at once. The squared coefficient
is negative, but it is not statistically distinguishable from zero once the
standard errors account for heteroskedasticity, and even taken at face value it
places the emissions peak at an income level roughly three times anything
observed. Within the range of the data, the relationship is a rising line. That
is a clean negative result and it is worth stating as one.

Caveats worth naming rather than burying, since this is a workshop and not a
paper. The specification ignores country fixed effects, so it mixes differences
between countries with changes within a country over time. It ignores the time
dimension entirely, though technology and energy prices moved a great deal
between 1970 and 2015. And 2397 rows lost to missing `GDP_percapita` are not
missing at random, since poorer countries report national accounts less
consistently. Any of the three could change the answer, and a serious version of
this analysis would address all of them.
